matching: Case-insensitive whole-phrase match with word boundaries, implemented as (?<!\w)term(?!\w) in scripts/score.py boundary_spans(). Boundaries are load-bearing: plain substring search would match 'qualified opinion' inside 'unqualified opinion', which is the opposite meaning and occurs 9 times in the v0.1 corpus. A tool flag counts as a term-of-art violation when its flagged span overlaps a whitelisted occurrence at 0.5 or more of the shorter span. Flags carrying a character offset are tested at that offset; flags carrying only quoted text are grouped by text and credited at most min(number of such flags, number of occurrences that actually collide), so one colliding occurrence cannot convict every flag sharing its wording. Morphological variants listed explicitly in the variants array; no stemming.

terms.citation: ISA 705 / AU-C 705 (pervasiveness threshold). NOT a PCAOB AS 3105 term.
terms.note: Term of art in the ISA and AICPA framework, where pervasiveness separates a qualified opinion from an adverse opinion. PCAOB AS 3105, which governs the issuer audits in this corpus, does not use that construction, so this entry is retained for cross-framework coverage rather than because PCAOB requires the word. Zero occurrences in the v0.1 corpus, so it contributes nothing to the current ToA metric. Reads as intensifier slop out of context. REVIEW: Rizwan to decide whether a PCAOB-audit corpus should carry ISA vocabulary at all.

Opinion type. Under PCAOB AS 3105 the auditor expresses a qualified 'except for' opinion when the financial statements are fairly presented apart from the effects of a specific matter, arising from either a GAAP departure or a scope limitation that does not preclude an opinion on the statements as a whole. PCAOB does not frame the choice using the ISA 'material but not pervasive' threshold; see the separate 'pervasive' entry. 'Qualified' here means 'with reservations / except for', near-opposite of the everyday sense of competent or eligible. Matching must exclude 'unqualified opinion', which is the opposite meaning and occurs 9 times in the v0.1 corpus.
Direct collision: 'comprehensive' is a Tier 1 hard-replace word in avoid-ai-writing.

terms.citation: FASB ASC 220 (Income Statement - Reporting Comprehensive Income); Master Glossary definition
terms.note: Defined GAAP term under ASC 220 and the conventional caption for the required statement. ASC 220 permits equivalent statement titles rather than prescribing one exact caption, so the defensible claim is that the TERM is defined, not that a specific statement name is mandated. Direct collision with Tier 1 'comprehensive' in avoid-ai-writing and stock_vocab in unslop; 25 occurrences in the v0.1 corpus, and the single largest source of ToA violations in the results.

terms.citation: SEC Regulation S-K Item 303 (MD&A liquidity and capital resources); Regulation G and Item 10(e) (non-GAAP measures must be consistently labelled and reconciled); covenant definitions in the filer's credit agreements
terms.note: Leverage as a financial metric, not as a verb. Where a filer defines 'managed leverage' or 'financial statement leverage' as a non-GAAP measure, Regulation G requires the label be used consistently and reconciled to GAAP, so renaming it is a disclosure problem rather than a style choice. 'Covenant leverage ratio' is defined contractually in the credit agreement. Direct collision with avoid-ai-writing Tier 1, whose table scopes the word to 'leverage (verb)' but whose detector regex does not honour that scoping and fires on these noun phrases in CAT and F filings. DELIBERATELY NOT PROTECTED: bare 'leverage', which in verb use ('leverage our position') is a fair flag and which these tools are right to catch. Protecting the bare word would excuse genuine slop and weaken the metric.
Required auditor communication for large accelerated filers since fiscal years ending on or after 2019-06-30, so it appears throughout the 2019-2021 corpus window.

deliberately_excluded.reason: avoid-ai-writing Tier 1 hard-replaces commence with start, and 'commenced' occurs in 4 corpus documents ('commenced operations', 'commenced an action'). It is formal legal register, NOT a defined term with a standard behind it, so protecting it would dilute the metric. Register collisions are reported separately in the README rather than counted as term-of-art violations. Wikipedia's 'Ineffective indicators' section makes the same point: formal prose is not an AI signal, but it is also not a regulatory requirement.
Fires in 3 corpus documents. Ordinary formal usage, no defined meaning, and the plain-language replacement ('use') is genuinely better writing. The tools are right here.
